teaching_path.action: Use q²−1=(q−1)(q+1) to separate the factors.
teaching_path.why_valid: The difference-of-squares identity is valid for all integers.
teaching_path.output: Product of the two neighbors of q.

teaching_path.action: If q is odd, q−1 and q+1 are even, with one multiple of four.
teaching_path.why_valid: They are even and differ by two, so their residues modulo4 are 0 and2.

teaching_path.action: If q is not divisible by3, one of its neighbors is; if q is divisible by3 neither neighbor is.
teaching_path.why_valid: Check the exhaustive q residues 0,1,2 modulo3.
teaching_path.output: 3 divides q²−1 iff 3 does not divide q.

teaching_path.action: Explain generally why proving both implications of a claim requires a warrant for each permitted and excluded case, without stating the target criterion.
teaching_path.why_valid: A sufficient example does not establish necessity; each direction needs a separate universal argument.
teaching_path.output: General two-direction proof method with independent factor checks; decide exact target classes in the later assessment.

misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Why do n=3 and n=5 behave differently even though both are odd?
misconceptions.repair: Oddness only guarantees 8; 3∤n is an independent required condition. Check both conditions, then multiply coprime factors.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Three true examples prove a universal iff.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What rules out the entire family of even n?
misconceptions.repair: Use parity for a universal contradiction; enumerate all modulus families.

exit_task.prompt: Prove that for any integer m, 8 divides m(m+2) exactly when m is even. Independently verify an unseen negative integer.

reasoning: If m=2t, then m(m+2)=4t(t+1), and t(t+1) is even.
If m is odd, then both m and m+2 are odd so their product is odd.
The argument also covers m=-4, giving product8.
answer.check: Check both parity classes and m=-4.

predict.prompt: A student checks n=5,7,11 and concludes all odd n make 24 divide n²−1. Does sampling prove a universal rule?
predict.defensible_answer: No: n=3 is odd and gives 8. The missing factor-of-three condition is decisive.

rubric.evidence_of: Necessity and sufficiency for all integers.

rubric.criterion: Justify factor8 for odd n and show even n cannot work.
Combine coprime factors and classify modulo6.

accepted: 24 divides n²−1 exactly when n is odd and 3∤n. If n odd, the two even neighbors differ by2, yielding factor8. If 3∤n a neighbor yields factor3. Conversely even n gives odd n²−1 and 3|n gives remainder2 mod3.
rejected: Every odd n works, because examples do.

task.prompt: Critique the odd-only claim, replace it with an exact iff condition for 24|(n²−1), and prove both directions.

route.ask: Test n=3; does it defeat the proposed odd-only rule?
Which half of the odd-only reasoning remains true for every odd n?
Which other residue class destroys factor3?

boundary_test.prompt: After repair, classify n=15 and n=17 using the corrected rule, then verify.
boundary_test.answer: n=15 fails because 3 divides it and 15²−1=224. n=17 passes and 17²−1=288=24×12.
boundary_test.confirms: Two-condition rule transfers to changed givens.

questions.stem: For all integers n, prove the exact necessary-and-sufficient criterion for 24 to divide n²−1. State all allowed residue classes modulo6 and prove both directions, including exceptions and a negative boundary.
conditions: n is any integer, including negative integers and zero.

reasoning: Sufficiency: for odd n, two even neighbors differ by2, giving factor8; if 3∤n a neighbor supplies factor3; coprimality yields24.
Necessity: even n has odd n²−1; a multiple of3 gives n²−1≡2 modulo3. Either cannot be divisible by24.
Thus n is odd and not divisible by3: exactly residues1 or5 modulo6.

reasoning_route.why_valid: An iff assertion needs necessity and sufficiency.

reasoning_route.action: Prove both condition families and both converses.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Odd n forces factor8, nonmultiples of3 force factor3; even n or multiples of3 give universal obstructions.

reasoning_route.action: Independently inspect modulo24 residues and negative/zero cases.
reasoning_route.why_valid: All residue classes of integers are exhausted.

answer.check: n=-1 yields0 (yes); n=0 yields -1 (no); n=3 yields8 (no); n=5 yields24 (yes). Enumerate residues modulo24.

questions.stem: The divisor changes to 48. Prove exactly which residue classes modulo24 give 48|(n²−1) for arbitrary integers n. Show why the earlier 24-rule fails on a permitted input.
conditions: n is any integer, including negative integers and zero.

reasoning: For odd n modulo8, residues1,3,5,7 square modulo16 to1,9,9,1. Even n cannot work. Thus 16 divides exactly when n mod8 is1 or7.
3 divides the expression exactly when n is not divisible by3. Combining the two restrictions gives n mod24 in {1,7,17,23}.
n=5 gives n²−1=24, invalidating naive reuse of the earlier rule.

reasoning_route.action: Classify when 16 divides n²−1 via odd residues mod8.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The four odd classes square modulo16 to1,9,9,1.

reasoning_route.action: Combine factor16 and factor3 and list modulo24 classes.
reasoning_route.why_valid: gcd(16,3)=1 and mod24 encodes both residue conditions.

reasoning_route.action: Exhaust all modulo24 classes and falsify old rule using n=5.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Every integer has one class, and n=5 is admissible.

answer.check: Check classes1,7,17,23 modulo24 and n=5 as old-rule false positive.

rubric.criterion: Combine with mod3 to get four mod24 classes.
